smt-2021-geometry-01.title: Law of cosines
smt-2021-geometry-01.body:
Let $B'$ be the folded position of $B$ (the reflection of $B$ in $AC$) and $x=\angle DCA$. Since $CD=8$ and $AD=6$, $\sin x=\frac35$ and $\cos x=\frac45$. Also $\angle BCA=90^\circ-x$ and so $\angle B'CA=90^\circ-x$ on the same side of $AC$ as $D$, giving $\angle B'CD=90^\circ-2x$ (in absolute value), with $\cos(90^\circ-2x)=\sin2x=2\cdot\frac35\cdot\frac45=\frac{24}{25}$.

In triangle $B'CD$ with $CB'=6$, $CD=8$: $B'D^2=36+64-2\cdot6\cdot8\cdot\frac{24}{25}=\frac{196}{25}$, so $B'D=\frac{14}5$.

**Answer: $\frac{14}5$**

smt-2021-geometry-02.title: Find $BD$
smt-2021-geometry-02.body:
Let $E,F$ be the feet of the perpendiculars from $A,B$ to $CD$. Then $EF=50$, so $DE+FC=75$. Sliding the two right triangles together gives a triangle with sides $45,60,75$ (a $3$-$4$-$5$ triangle), whose altitude to the side $75$ is $\frac{45\cdot60}{75}=36$, the height of the trapezoid. Then $DE=27$ and $CF=48$ (they sum to $75$). Thus $DF=27+50=77$ and $BD=\sqrt{36^2+77^2}=85$.

**The lens**

The two circles have radius $85$ and their centres are $85$ apart, so each passes through the other's centre. The common region is a lens of two equal circular segments, each cut off by a chord of length $85\sqrt3$ (an angle $120^\circ$ at the centre). Area of one segment: $\frac13\pi r^2-\frac{\sqrt3}{4}r^2$. The lens has area $2\left(\frac{\pi}{3}-\frac{\sqrt3}4\right)r^2$ with $r^2=7225$:
$$\frac{14450\pi}{3}-\frac{7225\sqrt3}{2}.$$

**Answer: $\frac{14450\pi}{3}-\frac{7225\sqrt3}{2}$**

smt-2021-geometry-03.title: Unit circle
smt-2021-geometry-03.body:
$\left(\frac{1-r^2}{1+r^2}\right)^2+\left(\frac{2r}{1+r^2}\right)^2=\frac{(1-r^2)^2+4r^2}{(1+r^2)^2}=1$, so the curve lies on the unit circle. $f(1/3)=\left(\frac45,\frac35\right)$ and $f(2)=\left(-\frac35,\frac45\right)$. The dot product is $-\frac{12}{25}+\frac{12}{25}=0$, so the points are perpendicular: a quarter of the circle, of length $\frac{2\pi}{4}=\frac\pi2$. The point $(-1,0)$ is not on this arc, so the arc lies on the curve.

**Answer: $\frac\pi2$**

smt-2021-geometry-04.title: Geometric series
smt-2021-geometry-04.body:
The $13$-$14$-$15$ triangle has area $84$, semiperimeter $21$, inradius $r=\frac{84}{21}=4$ and circumradius $R=\frac{13\cdot14\cdot15}{4\cdot84}=\frac{65}8$. The next triangle has the incircle as its circumcircle, so it is scaled by $\frac rR=\frac{32}{65}$. Hence $\sum A_iB_i=13\sum_{i\ge0}\left(\frac{32}{65}\right)^i=\frac{13}{1-32/65}=\frac{13\cdot65}{33}=\frac{845}{33}$.

**Answer: $\frac{845}{33}$**

smt-2021-geometry-05.title: Tangent addition
smt-2021-geometry-05.body:
$BE=\tan20^\circ$ and $DF=\tan25^\circ$, so $AE=1+\tan20^\circ$, $AF=1+\tan25^\circ$, and the area is $\frac12(1+\tan20^\circ)(1+\tan25^\circ)$. Since $\tan45^\circ=1=\frac{\tan20^\circ+\tan25^\circ}{1-\tan20^\circ\tan25^\circ}$, we have $\tan20^\circ+\tan25^\circ=1-\tan20^\circ\tan25^\circ$. So the product is $1+(\tan20^\circ+\tan25^\circ)+\tan20^\circ\tan25^\circ=2$, and the area is $1$.

**Answer: 1**

smt-2021-geometry-06.title: $G$ lies on a fixed circle
smt-2021-geometry-06.body:
Let the minor arc $CD$ of $\omega_A$ be $x^\circ$ and of $\omega_B$ be $y^\circ$. In $\triangle DEF$, $\angle DEF=\frac x2$ and $\angle DFE=\frac y2$, so $\angle EDF=180^\circ-\frac x2-\frac y2$. In triangles $ACD$, $BCD$: $\angle ADC=90^\circ-\frac x2$, $\angle BDC=90^\circ-\frac y2$, so $\angle ADB=180^\circ-\frac x2-\frac y2=\angle EDF$ (a fixed angle).

$AM\perp DE$ and $BN\perp DF$ (a line from a centre to the midpoint of a chord), so $DMGN$ is cyclic and $\angle MGN=180^\circ-\angle EDF=180^\circ-\angle ADB$. Hence $\angle AGB+\angle ADB=180^\circ$, and $G$ lies on the circumcircle of $\triangle ADB$, which has sides $AB=13$, $AD=14$, $BD=15$. Its circumradius is $\frac{13\cdot14\cdot15}{4\cdot84}=\frac{65}8$.

**Answer: $\frac{65}8$**

smt-2021-geometry-07.title: Compute the side of the $2n$-gon
smt-2021-geometry-07.body:
Let $O$ be the centre, $M$ the midpoint of a side of the original polygon, $N$ the nearest vertex, and $I$ an intersection point on that side. Then $MN=\frac12$, $\angle MON=\frac{180^\circ}{n}$, so $OM=\frac{1}{2\tan(180^\circ/n)}$. By symmetry $\angle MOI=\frac{90^\circ}{n}$ and $MI=OM\tan\frac{90^\circ}{n}$. With $t=\tan\frac{90^\circ}n$ and $\tan\frac{180^\circ}n=\frac{2t}{1-t^2}$: $MI=\frac{t(1-t^2)}{4t}=\frac{1-t^2}{4}$. The side of the $2n$-gon is $2MI=\frac{1-\tan^2(90^\circ/n)}{2}$. Matching with $\frac{1-\tan^210^\circ}2$ gives $\frac{90}{n}=10$, so $n=9$.

**Answer: 9**

smt-2021-geometry-08.title: $MEF$ is equilateral
smt-2021-geometry-08.body:
Since $\angle BEC=\angle BFC=90^\circ$, $E$ and $F$ lie on the circle with diameter $BC$ centred at $M$, so $ME=MF=\frac72$. Then $\angle BMF=180^\circ-2B$ and $\angle CME=180^\circ-2C$, so $\angle EMF=180^\circ-(180^\circ-2B)-(180^\circ-2C)=2(B+C)-180^\circ=180^\circ-2A$. By the law of cosines $\cos A=\frac{25+64-49}{80}=\frac12$, so $A=60^\circ$ and $\angle EMF=60^\circ$. Triangle $MEF$ is equilateral with side $\frac72$, so its area is $\frac{\sqrt3}{4}\cdot\frac{49}4=\frac{49\sqrt3}{16}$. Hence $a+b+c=49+3+16=68$.

**Answer: 68**

smt-2021-geometry-09.title: Tangential quadrilateral
smt-2021-geometry-09.body:
The centre $O$ of the rectangle is the midpoint of $AC$, so its distance to each external tangent of circles $A$ and $C$ is $\frac{r_1+r_3}{2}=\frac72$. Similarly its distance to the tangents of circles $B,D$ is $\frac{r_2+r_4}2=\frac72$ (since $r_1+r_3=r_2+r_4$). So $O$ is equidistant from all four sides: $WXYZ$ has an inscribed circle of radius $\frac72$. By Pitot's theorem $WX+YZ=XY+ZW=20$, so the perimeter is $40$, and the area is (semiperimeter)(inradius) $=20\cdot\frac72=70$.

**Answer: 70**

smt-2021-geometry-10.title: Areas from cosines
smt-2021-geometry-10.body:
Triangle $AEF$ is similar to $ABC$ with ratio $\cos A$, so $[AEF]=[ABC]\cos^2A$, and likewise $[BFD]=[ABC]\cos^2B$, $[CDE]=[ABC]\cos^2C$. Also $[DEF]=2[ABC]\cos A\cos B\cos C$. Since $[ABC]=[AEF]+[BFD]+[CDE]+[DEF]$, a consistent triangle has $\cos^2A=\frac{1}{[ABC]}$ etc.

Let $S=[ABC]$: then $\cos^2A=\frac1S$, $\cos^2C=\frac2S$, $\cos^2B=\frac{2-\sqrt3}{S}$. Take $S=4$: $\cos A=\frac12$, $\cos C=\frac{\sqrt2}2$, $\cos B=\frac{\sqrt6-\sqrt2}{4}$, i.e. $A=60^\circ$, $C=45^\circ$, $B=75^\circ$, which sum to $180^\circ$ and form an acute triangle. (This is the only solution with $S>5-\sqrt3$: eliminating $\cos A\cos B\cos C$ between the two relations gives $S(S-5+\sqrt3)^2=16-8\sqrt3$, which has the root $S=4$.)

So $[DEF]=4-1-2-(2-\sqrt3)=\sqrt3-1$.

**Answer: $\sqrt3-1$**
